title: Part 1: Introduction and interview (4–5 min)
summary: Short questions about you and familiar topics (work/studies, hometown, home, then 2–3 everyday topics). It tests whether you answer naturally and quickly with everyday vocabulary.
rule: Answer directly, add a reason, add one extra detail, then stop.

do: Match the tense of the question
Give a direct answer; paraphrase the question
Add one example or contrast, then stop
avoid: Repeating the question word for word

steps: Listen for the tense and the question word: 'Do you…?' (present habit), 'Did you… as a child?' (past), 'Have you ever…?' (present perfect plus a past-simple detail), 'Would you like to…?' (would + verb).

Sentence 1: give a direct answer. Paraphrase the question instead of repeating it ('Do you like parks?' → 'Yes, I'm quite a fan of green spaces…'). A softener is fine here: 'To be completely honest…', 'Generally speaking…', 'Absolutely…'.
Sentence 2: add a reason or a concrete detail ('…because…', 'mainly because…', 'The thing is…').
Sentence 3: add one extra point, an example or a contrast ('Also…', 'Plus…', 'On top of that…', 'However…', 'That said…'), then stop.
Aim for 2–3 sentences, about 20–30 seconds. Fit 1–2 topic collocations into the answer (e.g. 'a steady job', 'gain practical experience', 'a prime location').
Stop naturally and let the examiner move on. Part 1 rewards relaxed, natural answers, not speeches.
traps: One-word answers ('Yes.' / 'No, I don't.'). They give the examiner nothing to mark for LR or GRA.
Repeating the question word for word ('Do I like my hometown? Yes, I like my hometown…'). Paraphrase it instead.
Long, memorised mini-speeches. They sound rehearsed, and examiners lower the band for rehearsed speech.
Tense mismatch: answering a 'Did you…when you were a child?' question in the present tense.
Saying 'I don't know' and stopping. Say why you don't know or have never thought about it, and give a guess.
Overusing 'very', 'good', 'nice' and 'thing'. Swap them for precise words (e.g. 'really handy', 'a relaxed atmosphere').
tips: Pattern from the teacher's model answers: direct answer → reason/detail → extra point, example or contrast. Almost every model answer has three sentences.
Use 'I' and personal examples here. Contractions (I'm, don't, it's) and informal words like 'really' are fine in Speaking.
If you have no strong opinion, say so honestly and explain why ('I'm not really into watches, mainly because my phone tells me the time'). Honest answers sound more fluent than invented ones.
You may ask 'Sorry, could you repeat the question, please?'. In Part 1 the examiner can only repeat it, not explain it.
Practise every predicted Part 1 question for the season aloud. The teacher's instruction was 'Practice all the questions.'
Learn the model-answer collocations as chunks and answer in your own words. Don't recite the model answer.
example: Q: Is that a big city or a small place? → 'I would say it is a medium-sized city that is growing very fast because of new businesses. While it does not feel as crowded as a massive capital city, it still has everything you need, like big malls and efficient public transport. It gives you the advantages of city life without the terrible traffic.' (direct answer → contrast/detail → extra point; collocations: medium-sized city, public transport)
language: Also / Plus / On top of that …
If I had to pick one …

title: Part 2: Long turn / cue card (1 min prep + up to 2 min talk)
summary: You get a 'Describe…' card with four bullet points, 1 minute to make notes, then you speak alone for up to 2 minutes. It tests speaking at length, organising ideas and using narrative tenses.
rule: Cover every bullet and keep talking until the examiner says 'Thank you'.

do: Pick the first workable idea in 5 seconds
Open with 'I'd like to talk about…'
Bullets in order; longest on 'why / how you felt'
avoid: Writing full sentences in your notes
Present tense for a past story
remember: 1 min to prepare, up to 2 min to talk
~20–25 s per bullet, 30–40 s on the last

steps: Read the card (5 seconds) and decide quickly WHAT you will talk about. Pick the first workable idea. Don't waste the minute searching for the perfect story; you are marked on language, not truth.
Use the full minute to write notes: 1–3 keywords for each bullet (not sentences), in a column or 4 boxes, in the same order as the card.
Add 3–4 'show-off' phrases you want to use (an idiom, 2 collocations, a phrasal verb from the topic list, e.g. 'a hidden gem', 'to recharge my batteries', 'hit it off').
Mark the tenses: is the story in the past (past simple + past continuous + past perfect), a habit (present simple), or a plan (going to / would love to / I'm planning to)?
Open with one sentence that names the topic: 'I'd like to talk about…' / 'The person I'm going to describe is…'. Add one line of background (when / how you know it).
Cover the bullets in order, about 20–25 seconds on each of the first three. Use signposts: 'As for what we did…', 'Moving on to why…'.
Spend the most time (30–40 seconds) on the last bullet, usually 'why / how you felt'. Give two reasons and a specific moment or detail.
If you still have time, extend it: compare then and now, describe one specific moment in detail (what you saw, heard, felt), say what you'd do differently, or say whether you'd recommend it.
Keep talking until the examiner says 'Thank you'. Then answer the 1–2 short follow-up questions in one or two sentences.
traps: Stopping after 60–80 seconds. A short talk lowers FC. Plan an 'extension' idea (comparison, feelings, future) before you start.
Writing full sentences in the notes. You run out of prep time and end up reading aloud.
Ignoring a bullet point, or spending 1 minute on the first bullet ('where it is') and rushing the 'why'.
Answering a past-event card in the present tense ('Last year I go…'). Check the verb forms of the card ('when it happened', 'how you felt').
Changing the topic to a speech you memorised for a different card. Off-topic, memorised language is penalised.
Long silences while you look at the notes. Glance down, then keep talking with a linker ('Another thing I remember is…').
tips: Teacher's routine for every card: write one or two words per bullet, choose 3–4 phrases from the topic vocabulary (idioms, collocations, phrasal verbs, advanced words) and use 1–2 from each group.
The 'why / how you felt' bullet is where you can talk longest. Have two reasons ready plus a feeling word stronger than 'happy' (thrilled, relieved, proud, overwhelmed).

Narrative-tense chain for past stories: 'I had never got up that early before (past perfect), so when the alarm went off (past simple) it was still pitch black and everyone was sleeping (past continuous).'
Recycle: one prepared story can cover several cards (a trip can be 'a place you visited', 'a time you got up early', 'a plan you had to change').
If the card doesn't fit your life, adapt it or invent believable details. Saying 'I've never…' and stopping is the only wrong answer.

Structure option for people, places and objects: background → description (appearance/character) → experience/story → feelings. For events: background → what happened (beginning, middle, end) → result → feelings.
Structure option when a time frame helps: past (how it started / first time) → present (how it is now) → future (plans/hopes).
example: Card: 'Describe a plan you had to change.' Notes: PLAN – weekend hiking trip, mountains, 3 friends | WHY – storm forecast, eleventh hour | NEW – museum + café in town, 'play it by ear' | FEEL – disappointed → relieved, 'a blessing in disguise', next time contingency plan. Talk: 'I'd like to talk about a hiking trip I'd been planning for weeks with three friends from university… Unfortunately, at the eleventh hour we found out a storm was coming… So we decided to play it by ear and stayed in town… To be honest, I was pretty disappointed at first, but looking back it was a blessing in disguise because…'
language: This happened about two years ago, when …

title: Part 3: Discussion (4–5 min)
summary: Abstract questions linked to the Part 2 theme, about people and society, comparing past and present, and speculating about the future. It tests giving, supporting and balancing opinions.
rule: Opinion → reason → example → other side → short close.

do: Give a direct opinion, then explain why
Add an example from your country
Add another view, then close briefly
avoid: Talking only about yourself, not people

steps: Identify the question function: opinion ('Do you think…?'), compare ('What's the difference between…?'), cause ('Why do people…?'), advantage/disadvantage, future ('Will… in the future?'), or solution ('How can…?').
Buy 1–2 seconds naturally if you need to: 'That's an interesting question…', 'I've never really thought about it, but…'.
1. Opinion: answer directly and give your overall view ('I'd say that…', 'On the whole, I think…').
2. Reason: explain why, using cause-and-effect language ('This is mainly because…', 'which means that…').
3. Example: give a specific situation, from your country, your generation or people you know ('For instance, in my country…', 'Take my grandparents, for example…').
4. Alternative view or contrast: 'On the other hand…', 'Having said that…', 'It depends on…'. This shows the range of a band 7+ answer.
5. Close: link back to the question in one short sentence ('So, overall…', 'Ultimately…', 'In short…').
Aim for about 40–60 seconds (5–7 sentences). If the examiner interrupts to move on, that's normal and not a bad sign.
traps: Talking only about yourself. Part 3 is about people in general, so use 'many people', 'the younger generation', 'in my country', 'in the past… whereas nowadays…'.
One-sentence opinions with no reason or example, which caps FC and LR.
Very extreme claims ('Everyone hates…', 'Technology will destroy…'). Hedge instead: 'tend to', 'in many cases', 'it's likely that'.
Using 'will' for every future idea. Vary it: 'is likely to', 'I'd imagine that…', 'it might well…', 'there's a good chance that…'.
Panicking at an unfamiliar topic. Say so, then reason it out aloud. Hesitation about ideas is acceptable, but hesitation about language is what lowers the band.
Reusing the same linker ('and… and… and also…'). Vary the connectives.
tips: Teacher's model-answer pattern (6–7 sentences): direct view → reason 1 → reason 2 or the other side (On the other hand / However / In contrast) → example (For instance…) → close (Ultimately / Therefore / Consequently / In short).

Recycle the Part 2 idioms and collocations in Part 3 (e.g. 'get away from it all', 'a hard pill to swallow', 'call a rain check'). The teacher's Part 3 answers do exactly this, so the Part 2 vocabulary pays off twice.
You may ask the examiner to rephrase or explain a Part 3 question: 'Sorry, do you mean… or…?'
For 'compare past and present' questions: 'In the past…, whereas these days…', 'Back in my parents' day…', 'Compared to twenty years ago…'.
For 'future' questions: give a prediction plus a reason plus a condition ('I'd imagine… because…, although that depends on…').
For 'advantages' questions, name 2 advantages briefly rather than listing 5, then develop one with an example.
example: Q: Will online social media replace face-to-face communication? → Opinion: 'I don't think online platforms will ever fully replace talking in person.' → Reason: 'Humans have a natural need to be physically close to the people they care about.' → Contrast: 'While video calls are helpful, they cannot replace real eye contact or body language.' → Example: 'A smartphone screen can never act as a real shoulder to cry on when you're going through a hard time.' → Close: 'Because of this, face-to-face talking will always be the most important way we connect.'
language: I'd say that … / On the whole, …
On the other hand, … / Having said that, …

title: All parts: fluency, pronunciation and what examiners reward
summary: How the four equally weighted criteria (Fluency & Coherence, Lexical Resource, Grammatical Range & Accuracy, Pronunciation) are applied, and the habits that raise or lower the band in every part.
rule: Keep talking smoothly; clear, natural English beats big words.

do: Use topic collocations; paraphrase missing words
Fix a mistake quickly and carry on
remember: 4 equal criteria: FC, LR, GRA, Pronunciation

steps: Fluency & Coherence (FC): keep speaking without long pauses and link ideas logically with varied connectives (because, so, although, which means, on top of that, having said that). Band 7 = 'speaks at length without noticeable effort'.

Lexical Resource (LR): use topic collocations and some less common or idiomatic items naturally (e.g. 'a hidden gem', 'at the eleventh hour'). If you lack a word, paraphrase it ('the thing you use to…'). Band 7 needs 'some less common and idiomatic items' and awareness of collocation.

Grammatical Range & Accuracy (GRA): mix simple and complex sentences, using relative clauses (which/who), conditionals (If I had…, I would…), passives, present perfect, narrative tenses and comparatives. Band 7 needs 'frequently error-free' complex sentences.
Pronunciation (P): be easy to understand. Stress key words, chunk phrases, let your intonation rise and fall naturally, and pronounce word endings (-ed, -s). Speed matters less than clarity.
Self-correction: if you notice a mistake, fix it quickly ('I go… I went there last year') and carry on. Don't restart the whole sentence or apologise.
Fillers: natural ones ('Well…', 'Let me think…', 'Actually…') are fine in moderation. Silence and 'ehh… ehh…' are not.
Record yourself in the app's Speaking practice, then listen back for long pauses, repeated words (very, good, thing, like) and tense errors.
traps: What lowers the band: long pauses while searching for words; repeating the same words and linkers; slow, word-by-word speech (FC 5).
Memorised or rehearsed answers that don't fit the question. Examiners spot them, and they can't be credited as evidence of your real level.
Using 'big words' or idioms incorrectly or in the wrong register ('It's raining cats and dogs' squeezed into every answer). Inappropriate or forced idioms count against you, not for you.
Only short, simple sentences (caps GRA around 5), or attempting complex sentences you can't control.
Mumbling, swallowing word endings, flat monotone delivery or speaking too fast to be clear (lowers P).
Too much self-correction. Correcting every small slip breaks your fluency more than the slip itself.
tips: Band 6 → 7 shift: answer at length without effort, use a few less common words and idioms correctly, produce many error-free complex sentences, and use connectives flexibly.
Band 8: hesitation is only about ideas (not words); idiomatic language is used skilfully; most sentences are error-free; you are easy to understand throughout.
Learn vocabulary as chunks (collocations), not single words. Chunks also make your rhythm and pronunciation sound more natural.
Contractions, personal stories and informal words like 'really' are fine in Speaking (unlike Writing Task 2).
A mock score is a floor, not a forecast. The teacher noted that mock speaking scores may not fully reflect real exam conditions.
The Speaking test is face to face (or by video call) even in the computer-delivered exam. Practise answering to a real person, not only to a screen.
Keep eye contact, sit naturally and treat it as a conversation. Interruptions by the examiner are normal timing, not a sign of a bad answer.
example: Self-correction done well: 'When I was a child I go… I used to go to my grandparents' village every summer, which was where I first learned to ride a bike.' (quick fix, then a complex sentence with 'used to' and a relative clause)
